decisions.question: Do Switzerland, Germany and Austria run on one store with Shopify Markets, on a store each, or on a hybrid?

options.pros: One catalogue, one admin and one theme, with currency, language, domain and pricing set per market
options.cons: Every market shares one theme, one app estate and one admin; per-market theme customisation starts at the Advanced plan

assessment.plan: No plan step: country and region markets, per-market currency, domains and price lists run from Basic upwards.
assessment.run_cost: One Shopify subscription and one app estate for all three markets — no duplication in the monthly bill.
assessment.build_effort: Configuration, not development: markets, domains, price lists and language publishing.
assessment.time_to_launch: Fastest of the three — one store to build, test and sign off.
assessment.who_can_change_it: The client adds a market, a price list or a language in the admin without a developer.
assessment.operational_load: One admin and one catalogue for the DACH team; orders from all three markets in one place.
assessment.reversibility: A market can be split into its own store later, at the cost of a migration and redirects.
assessment.limits: All markets share one theme, one app estate and one admin; per-market theme customisation needs Advanced or higher.
assessment.multi_market: CH in CHF, DE and AT in EUR, each on its own domain with manual price lists — exactly the case Markets is built for.
assessment.b2b: B2B companies live on the same store and see the same catalogue structure, with their own catalogs and price lists.
assessment.checkout: One checkout configuration across the three markets; local payment methods differ by market, not by store.
assessment.data_privacy: One customer record and one data estate; the ERP and PIM integrate once instead of three times.
assessment.performance_seo: Subfolder or country domains inherit one domain authority; one migration and one redirect map at launch.

options.pros: Hard separation of data, staff, finance and local operations
options.cons: Requires Shopify Plus, and nothing is shared: every catalogue, theme and app change is repeated in each store

assessment.plan: Shopify Plus only — expansion stores are a Plus contract feature.
assessment.run_cost: Apps and theme licences are billed per store, so the app estate is paid three times.
assessment.build_effort: Three builds, or one build repeated three times, plus the work to keep them aligned.
assessment.time_to_launch: Slowest: three stores to configure, test and sign off before launch.
assessment.who_can_change_it: The client can change each store, but every change has to be made three times.
assessment.operational_load: Three admins, three catalogues, three inventory set-ups; orders are not in one place.
assessment.reversibility: Merging stores later is a full migration of products, customers and order history.
assessment.limits: Nothing is synced between stores: settings, products, collections and inventory are all separate.
assessment.multi_market: Hard separation per country, which nothing in ACME’s answers asks for: one entity, one range, one team.
assessment.b2b: B2B would sit in one of the stores, or become a fourth — another store to run.
assessment.checkout: Three checkout configurations to keep identical, and three sets of payment settings.
assessment.data_privacy: Customer data is split across three stores; the ERP integrates three times and reconciliation gets harder.
assessment.performance_seo: Three domains each building their own authority from zero, and three redirect maps at launch.

options.option: Hybrid — a core store plus a separate store for one market
options.pros: Isolates a market that genuinely diverges without duplicating the ones that do not
options.cons: Two estates to run for as long as the exception lasts; also requires Shopify Plus

assessment.plan: Shopify Plus, for the same reason: the second store is an expansion store.
assessment.run_cost: Two subscriptions and two app estates instead of one.
assessment.build_effort: One build plus a second, smaller one — justified only when a market genuinely diverges.
assessment.time_to_launch: Between the two: the core store can launch first and the exception follow.
assessment.who_can_change_it: Same as one store for the core markets; the exception is maintained separately.
assessment.operational_load: Two admins for a business that runs one team — the cost lands on the client every day.
assessment.reversibility: Easier to fold back than three stores, but still a migration.
assessment.limits: Carries the expansion-store isolation for the market that leaves the core store.
assessment.multi_market: The right answer when one market has its own entity, range or team. None of ACME’s three does.
assessment.b2b: Would make sense if wholesale were its own operation; ACME runs it with the same team.
assessment.checkout: Two checkout configurations to keep aligned.
assessment.data_privacy: The separated market’s customer and order data sits outside the main estate.
assessment.performance_seo: The separated market builds its own domain authority.

decisions.decision: One store with Shopify Markets for CH, DE and AT
decisions.rationale: The client stated CHF and EUR checkout currencies, manual per-market price lists and three German-speaking markets. The engine derived one selling entity (ACME Watches AG invoices in all three markets), the same range everywhere and one central team, so no business fact separates the markets. Managed Markets is not eligible: the business is based in Switzerland, and Shopify documents eligibility for the continental United States and certain stores in Canada and the United Kingdom only. Confidence is to_validate: the entity mapping and the range relationship were assumed rather than stated, which is what exit rule 11.23 flags for the topology workshop.

why_not.reason: Nothing separates the markets by selling entity, range or team, so a second store would duplicate every catalogue, theme and app change for no benefit — and would require Shopify Plus
No single market diverges enough to leave the core store; DE and AT share the entity, the range and the team with CH

why_not.option: Managed Markets (Global-e as merchant of record)
why_not.reason: Not eligible: the business is based in Switzerland, outside the documented US, Canada and United Kingdom eligibility

impact.technical: One Shopify store, one theme and one app estate, with markets carrying currency, domain, language and price lists; no cross-store synchronisation to build.
impact.project: One build, one QA matrix and one release train. Per-market theme content would move the plan to Advanced, so it is scoped as a decision point rather than an assumption.
impact.merchant: One admin for the whole DACH business: the team edits products, prices and content once, and sees orders from all three markets in one place.
impact.customer: A local domain, local currency and local language in each market, with one checkout experience shared across them.

decisions.question: Native Shopify B2B or a wholesale app?

options.pros: Company accounts, catalogs and price lists in the same store

assessment.plan: Company-specific catalogs need Plus; up to three shared catalogs run from Basic.
assessment.run_cost: No app subscription — it is part of the platform.
assessment.build_effort: Configuration of companies, locations, catalogs and payment terms; no custom build.
assessment.time_to_launch: Launches with the store; nothing to integrate first.
assessment.who_can_change_it: The sales team manages companies, price lists and terms in the admin.
assessment.operational_load: One catalogue and one order flow for both audiences; no second system to reconcile.
assessment.reversibility: Native data stays in Shopify, so moving later is an export rather than an extraction.
assessment.limits: B2B checkout does not support accelerated payments, subscriptions or legacy customer accounts.
assessment.b2b: Companies, company locations, catalogs, net terms and PO numbers — the documented native model.
assessment.checkout: B2B buyers use the same checkout with B2B rules; the accelerated-payment limits apply to them.

options.cons: Separate pricing logic and checkout limits

assessment.plan: Runs on any plan, so it can avoid the Plus step for company-specific pricing.
assessment.run_cost: A permanent monthly subscription, usually banded by order volume or company count.
assessment.build_effort: Install and configure, plus the work to make it agree with the theme and the ERP.
assessment.time_to_launch: Comparable, unless the app needs its own data model to be populated first.
assessment.who_can_change_it: The sales team works in the app’s own admin, not in Shopify’s.
assessment.operational_load: A second place to maintain customers and prices, and a second support relationship.
assessment.reversibility: Leaving the app means extracting its data model and rebuilding the native one.
assessment.limits: The vendor’s roadmap decides what changes; app data often sits outside the Shopify objects.
assessment.b2b: Can cover company-specific pricing without Plus, at the cost of a parallel data model.
assessment.checkout: Some wholesale apps route through draft orders rather than the standard checkout.

decisions.decision: Native Shopify B2B on Shopify Plus
decisions.rationale: Fixed-tier price lists and account approval are native; the target plan is Plus.

decisions.question: How do ERP and PIM exchange data with Shopify?

options.option: Client iPaaS with Admin GraphQL API and webhooks
options.pros: Uses the client platform; retries and monitoring

assessment.plan: No plan requirement: the Admin API and webhooks are available on every plan.
assessment.run_cost: The client already licenses the iPaaS, so no new recurring cost lands on this project.
assessment.build_effort: Flows built in a tool the client’s team already knows, against documented APIs.
assessment.time_to_launch: Parallel to the store build; no bespoke deployment to stand up first.
assessment.who_can_change_it: The client’s integration team changes a flow without touching Shopify code.
assessment.operational_load: Monitoring and retries live in the iPaaS the client already operates.
assessment.reversibility: Flows can be rebuilt elsewhere; nothing is locked inside a custom app.
assessment.limits: Admin API rate limits and bulk-operation constraints apply; large catalogue syncs need bulk operations.
assessment.data_privacy: Order and customer data crosses into the iPaaS, so the processor list and retention have to cover it.

assessment.plan: No plan requirement, unless it embeds Shopify Functions, which need Plus in a custom app.
assessment.run_cost: No licence, but hosting and maintenance are a permanent line.
assessment.build_effort: A full build: auth, webhooks, retries, observability and deployment.
assessment.time_to_launch: Adds a workstream that has to be ready before the integrations can be tested.
assessment.operational_load: The client owns uptime, error handling and Shopify API version upgrades.
assessment.reversibility: Owned outright, but replacing it is a rebuild rather than a reconfiguration.
assessment.limits: API versioning forces an upgrade cadence; Shopify deprecates versions on a published schedule.
assessment.data_privacy: Data stays in infrastructure the client controls, which simplifies the processor position.

decisions.decision: Client iPaaS flows on the Admin GraphQL API and webhooks
decisions.rationale: The client already runs an iPaaS for ERP and PIM.

integrations.error_handling: Retries with dead-letter queue and daily reconciliation
